title: Use sensitivity labels to improve AI Agents accuracy and organizational alignment
summary: A Fabric Updates Blog post proposing a design pattern where an AI skill or agent reads a Fabric item's existing Purview sensitivity label not just to enforce access control, but as a context signal that changes how the agent responds — for example summarizing rather than detailing Confidential content, or declining to touch Highly Confidential material even for users who technically have access.
audience: Builders designing Fabric AI skills/agents who need the agent's answers to reflect organizational judgment about data sensitivity, not just permission checks.
why_it_matters: Access control alone does not stop an authorized-but-inappropriate answer from mixing public and confidential context in one response; using sensitivity labels as an in-skill behavioral signal is a pattern architects can reuse across any Fabric agent that reasons over classified content.
takeaways: The core idea is repurposing sensitivity labels an organization already maintains as a second signal beyond access control: guidance for what the agent should do with the data, not just whether it may touch it.
Labels remain available to agents through the same public sensitivity-label APIs already generally available for Fabric, so this is a consumption pattern rather than a new labeling mechanism.

The worked example is a report-analysis skill with three label tiers (General, Confidential, Highly Confidential) each mapped to a different response behavior — full detail, summary-only, or executive-only escalation.
This pattern does not change what a user is permitted to see; it changes how the agent composes an answer from the sources it's already allowed to read.
The recommended starting point is a single focused skill/scenario, validated for whether label-based guidance measurably improves answer relevance before wider rollout.

claims.text: Sensitivity labels in Fabric, defined in Microsoft Purview, classify Fabric and Power BI items (reports, semantic models, lakehouses) into levels such as General, Confidential, Highly Confidential, or custom labels, and are exposed through public APIs enabling programmatic access by agents and automated workflows.

An AI skill or agent can read an item's sensitivity label as a guidance signal separate from permission checks, using it to decide how appropriate a given piece of data is for the current question rather than only whether the user is allowed to see it.

Without label-aware guidance, a report-analysis skill treats all attached reports equally, which can cause it to blend public and confidential content into a single answer to a general question, mixing contexts the organization intended to keep separate.

In the article's worked pattern, label-based rules are defined per tier: General-labeled reports get full analysis with charts and data points; Confidential reports return only a summary to authorized users with access logged; Highly Confidential reports are restricted to cleared executives and produce only high-level briefings with all access tracked.

Label-based response rules do not expand or restrict what a user can access; a user still sees only the reports they are already permitted to see, but the agent changes how much detail it surfaces from those permitted sources based on label tier.

The recommended adoption sequence is to first ensure the data a skill depends on is consistently labeled, since unlabeled data provides the skill with no signal to act on, then define per-label handling rules, then apply the rules within one narrowly scoped skill before expanding further.
